results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 16 prose units map one-to-one and in order to p01-p16, each summary agreeing with its spec paragraph's controlling idea; the three callouts are house-format apparatus and match no spec paragraph.

The outliner marked two units. The KEY POINTS callout holds three bullets by the house format and is not a spec paragraph. How to Use ¶2 (p03) covers the table format and that Veldmark rows are fiction, which is exactly p03's single controlling idea (how to read a section and its rows).
p01 supports G1/G2; p02-p03 and the section lead paragraphs with their tables support G3; p14 supports G3; p15-p16 support G2.

The p01 example is explained (a report adding the three counts nothing useful); each of the ten tables is introduced by a lead paragraph saying what its terms cover and which chapters own them; the draft has no figures or quotations.

Every declared transition is carried by the unit's first sentence: elaboration into How to Use ('The sections follow the book's structure'), sequence into Reading and Parts I, III, IV, VI, VIII, elaboration into Part II ('Inside that business sits the thing being sold'), cause_effect into Part V ('Matching strangers also draws fraud ... so'), place into Part VII ('Every part so far runs on one distributed system'), contrast into Veldmark ('this last section is different'), conclusion_summary into the index and p15, additional_support into p16.

results.spec_locus: /flow (grouping by part; Part VI owns contact, conversation and lead)
results.draft_locus: Part I — Marketplace table, Liquidity row (also Time to first contact and Contact rate / sell-through rows)
results.quote: a listing receives a qualified contact and a buyer finds a suitable, available listing
results.finding: 'Contact', the page's headline term, is used as a technical term from the opening paragraph and throughout Part I, but its row is five sections later in Part VI, with no pointer; Part III already gives such a pointer for 'lead' ('the professional's side of the lead that Part VI defines'). The spec's part order is sound; the draft lacks the forward pointer at first use. ('Lead' in Part I's Lead-generation marketplace row has the same gap.)
results.corroborated_by: first flow reader, item A10; second flow reader, item B20

results.quote: When a chapter and this page disagree, one of them needs correcting, and the chapter's worked example is the better test of which.
results.finding: The clipped ending 'the better test of which' had to be re-read (first flow reader, A13).

results.draft_locus: FAILURE PATTERNS callout vs. Reading the Book table, Vanity Liquidity row
results.quote: when "contact" means a message in one warehouse, a lead in another and a phone reveal in a third, the group steers on numbers that cannot be compared
results.finding: The callout describes Vanity Liquidity as inconsistent definitions, while its row says 'measures listings and visits instead of matches, contacts and sales'; the mismatch made the reader check whether these were the same pattern (first flow reader, A14).

results.draft_locus: KEY POINTS callout, first bullet; latency rows in Parts II, III, IV and V
results.quote: the rows around a term carry the contrasts that cause real design errors
results.finding: The latency family (sold-to-gone latency, freshness SLA, platform/source latency, insertion/removal latency, alert latency, time to action) is spread over four sections with no cross-reference, so the reader could not tell whether sold-to-gone and removal latency are the same measure (first flow reader, A15). This follows from the declared grouping by part.

results.draft_locus: Part VII — Platform table, Platform funding models row
results.quote: showback of usage-based cost without charging, chargeback by usage
results.finding: 'Chargeback' here is a platform-cost term, unlike the card chargeback of Part VI; the index disambiguates but the row does not, and the reader briefly read it as the payments term (first flow reader, A16).

results.draft_locus: Part VIII — Leadership table, Stressor analysis row (before the Stressor / residue / attractor row)

results.finding: 'Attractor' and 'residue' are used one row before the row that defines them; the reader read on, then went back. The row title also lists residue before attractor while the definition takes them in the other order.

results.draft_locus: Part V — Trust table, Demotion row (and Notice and action, Appeal, Statement of reasons rows)
results.quote: Under DSA Article 17 it is a restriction that needs a statement of reasons

(P2B Regulation and the Omnibus Directive are also cited in Part IV before their Part V rows, but are named in full.)

results.draft_locus: Part VII — Platform table, Model governance / decision tiers row
results.quote: scaled to the decision it makes: inform, order, gate or commit
results.finding: The four decision tiers are named without a gloss; 'order' is ambiguous (ranking or purchase order) and is not defined elsewhere on the page.
The opening paragraph leads with a concrete hook (the dealer message that is a contact, a conversation and perhaps a lead) and the reason for the page; none of the listed weak patterns.
p15 synthesizes and calls back, p16 hands off; no 'in conclusion', no new idea, no rephrased thesis alone.

p15: one meaning and one owning chapter per term, so the dealer message is counted on purpose; settle a term before it goes into a metric, contract or policy, and check regulatory or company terms against their current source.
p15 returns to 'the buyer's first message to the dealer' as a contact, a conversation or a lead, 'on purpose, never by accident'.

The cold reader of the opening named the order (reading vocabulary, one section per part, Veldmark names, alphabetical index) and the use (look up, read neighbors for contrasts, follow the owning-chapter link, treat disagreement as an error, check regulatory and company terms). It could not say what the reading vocabulary contains, how many parts there are or what Veldmark is; the spec's roadmap defers that detail to p02, so the criterion is met.
The reader defined contact, conversation and lead and the publication state versus the enforcement overlay as expected, and named messaging-and-leads and listing-aggregate as owners.
The reader found ATO through the index under A, expanded it as account takeover, reached the Part V — Trust row and named fraud-prevention and identity-and-verification.
